
# **Olist Data Warehouse — Snowflake \+ dbt**

### **Overview**

This project uses the public Brazilian ecommerce dataset of orders made at [Olist Store](http://www.olist.com/). The dataset has information of 100k orders from 2016 to 2018 made at multiple marketplaces in Brazil. Its features allow viewing an order from multiple dimensions: from order status, price, payment and freight performance to customer location, product attributes and finally reviews written by customers.

The goal of the project was to build the pipeline which can take the raw data from an Amazon S3-bucket and turn it into business-ready insights while following a star-architecture with fact and dimension tables operating on two grain levels.

Initially the data has been put into the Amazon S3-bucket and I have connected it to the Snowflake through stage and storage integration.

### **From S3 to Snowflake**

The seven CSV files live in `s3://<bucket>/olist/`. A storage integration lets Snowflake assume an IAM role with read-only access to that folder; AWS trusts only Snowflake's principal together with a specific external ID.

```sql
CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3\_olist\_int  
  TYPE \= EXTERNAL\_STAGE  
  STORAGE\_PROVIDER \= 'S3'  
  ENABLED \= TRUE  
  STORAGE\_AWS\_ROLE\_ARN \= 'arn:aws:iam::\<account\_id\>:role/snowflake-olist-role'  
  STORAGE\_ALLOWED\_LOCATIONS \= ('s3://\<bucket\>/olist/');

CREATE STAGE olist.raw.olist\_stage  
  URL \= 's3://\<bucket\>/olist/'  
  STORAGE\_INTEGRATION \= s3\_olist\_int  
  FILE\_FORMAT \= csv\_ff;

COPY INTO olist.raw.orders  
  FROM @olist.raw.olist\_stage  
  PATTERN \= '.\*olist\_orders\_dataset.\*';
```

**dbt setup**  
After that, I have connected Snowflake and dbt by creating a service-user for dbt within Snowflake.  
Then I prepared `profiles.yml`: the account identifier and the private key path are read from environment variables, dbt signs in with key-pair authentication, and the key file is excluded from Git via `.gitignore`.

**Data model**  
The architecture I chose was star because I approached this project with business questions touching two different layers of data (order deliveries and sales in general). So this setup influenced my choice of grain and how many fact tables I have created in this project \- 2 fact tables(order items and order fulfillment) and 4 dimension tables(seller, product, date, customer). Dimensions are denormalized and that allows for a flatter architecture which is known for a more optimal query performance and more importantly ease of use as it allows performing fewer joins.

| Table  | Type | Grain (one row \=)  | Primary key  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `fct_order_items` | Transactional fact | One item within an order | `order_item_sk` |
| `fct_order_fulfillment` | Accumulating snapshot fact | One order, from purchase to delivery | `order_id` |
| `dim_customer` | Dimension, SCD Type 2 | One version of a customer | `customer_sk` |
| `dim_product` | Dimension, category flattened in | One product | `product_sk` |
| `dim_seller` | Dimension | One seller | `seller_sk` |
| `dim_date` | Date dimension, role-playing | One day  | `date_key (YYYYMMDD)` |

### **Why two fact tables**

Price, product and seller belong to a single order item, while delivery dates and payments belong to the order as a whole. Putting both into one table would repeat order-level values on every item row and inflate totals and averages: an order with five items would count five times in the average delivery time. So each level of detail gets its own fact table, and each table answers its own group of questions.

![dbt lineage graph](images/dbt-dag.png)

The heart of the dbt part of the project is the dbt\_project.yml, the main observations for this file are that I created views within a designated “staging” schema and tables within the designated “marts” schema.

Before the main part of the dbt transformation work, I have installed the dbt utils package by listing it in the packages.yml to generate a calendar for dim\_date and surrogate keys:  
![packages.yml](images/dbt_utils_screenshot.png)

During the staging my goal was to leave the data as untouched as I could. This is why the only actions I made were to convert the columns into the right data types and also trim, and get the right case of letters by using trim, initcap, upper functions.![Staging model stg_orders](images/staging_screenshot.png)
try\_to\_timestamp allowed for conversion without throwing out an error in the event of an unsuccessful conversion (null instead). 

Sources.yml file let me specify the names and the schemas where the raw data was.![sources.yml](images/source_screenshot.png)

**Customer snapshot**   
Additionally, I have added a customers\_snapshot.sql to track the location changes of the clients.![Customer snapshot](images/cust_snapshot.png)
Because client’s location is an important part of the analysis, I decided to add the SCD-2 to see their previous locations and what is the most up-to-date one:  
![dim_customer with SCD Type 2](images/scd_2_1.png)

Working with date required adding a macro which would help convert any timestamp into a `YYYYMMDD` key and fallback to `19000101` for missing dates.

![date_key macro](images/macro.png)

### **Facts**

Facts carry only keys and numbers; descriptive attributes stay in the dimensions. The customer key is looked up as of the purchase date, so every order points to the customer version that was valid at that moment:

left join {{ ref('dim\_customer') }} dc  
    on  c.customer\_unique\_id \= dc.customer\_unique\_id  
    and o.purchased\_at \>= dc.valid\_from  
    and o.purchased\_at \<  dc.valid\_to

## **Data quality**

Every key is tested, every fact-to-dimension link is tested, and row counts reconcile with the source.

### **Tests**

`dbt build` runs models and their tests in dependency order (21 data tests in total):

* `unique` and `not_null` on the primary key of every dimension and fact;  
* `relationships` from each foreign key in the facts to its dimension, so no fact row points to a missing customer, product, seller or date;  
* a custom test, `assert_no_negative_prices`, that fails if any price or freight value is negative.

### **Row-count reconciliation**

On the original data, every table matches the source exactly:

| Table | Rows | Check |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `fct_order_items` | 112,650 | Same as source order items — no rows lost or duplicated by joins |
| `fct_order_fulfillment` | 99,441 | One row per source order |
| `dim_customer` | 96,097 | 96,096 unique customers \+ Unknown |
| `dim_product` | 32,952 | 32,951 products \+ Unknown |
| `dim_seller` | 3,096 | 3,095 sellers \+ Unknown |

## **SCD Type 2 in action**

The source data is static, so a change was simulated to prove the history works end to end.

I moved one customer to Rio de Janeiro in the raw data, ran `dbt snapshot`, created a new test order for the same customer and rebuilt the models. The 2018 order is still linked to the old version of the customer (Campinas, `is_current = No`), while the new order is linked to the current one (Rio de Janeiro, `is_current = Yes`).

![SCD Type 2 demo query result](images/scd_2_2.png)

**How to run**  
1\. Load the CSV files into OLIST.RAW (see "From S3 to Snowflake").  
2\. pip install dbt-snowflake  
3\. Set SNOWFLAKE\_ACCOUNT and SNOWFLAKE\_PRIVATE\_KEY\_PATH.  
4\. dbt deps  
5\. dbt build
